title: NLRB v. New Vista Nursing and Rehabilitation
lead: A nursing-home labor dispute became a challenge to recess appointments when the appellate court questioned whether the deciding Board group contained three lawful members.

actors.name: New Vista Nursing and Rehabilitation
actors.role: Newark employer contesting representation of licensed practical nurses

actors.name: National Labor Relations Board
actors.role: Agency that ordered New Vista to bargain

actors.name: Craig Becker, Wilma Liebman, and Hayes
actors.role: Members of the group issuing the original order

proceedings: Regional director and Board: nurses covered; union won election; refusal to bargain led to unfair-labor-practice order.
Third Circuit: vacated original and reconsideration orders 2–1 because Becker’s appointment left the original group improperly composed.
limits: This is the May 2013 panel stage. The later Supreme Court Noel Canning decision permitted intrasession appointments. Nurses’ supervisory status, the vacancies-happen issue, and later groups’ appointments were not decided by the majority.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A representation dispute produces a reviewable refusal-to-bargain order
sections.cue: Begin with the workers and the original deciding group.
paragraphs: New Vista operated a nursing and rehabilitation center in Newark. In January 2011, a healthcare workers’ union sought to represent its licensed practical nurses. New Vista argued that the nurses were supervisors excluded from protection under the National Labor Relations Act, or NLRA. The regional director disagreed, the National Labor Relations Board upheld the representation determination, and the union won an election.

New Vista refused to bargain, prompting an unfair-labor-practice charge and summary-judgment motion. That refusal supplied the ordinary route to judicial review because the representation ruling was not directly reviewable. A unanimous Board order dated August 26, 2011, came from Chairman Wilma Liebman and Members Craig Becker and Hayes. Liebman left the next day. New Vista contended that later mailing meant the order issued only after her departure.

sections.title: Reconsideration creates further appointment objections
sections.cue: Track the administrative orders without deciding all their challenges.
paragraphs: New Vista sought reconsideration in September while the Board sought appellate enforcement. Record filing was held in abeyance during reconsideration. After a December 30 denial, New Vista raised objections about recusal and expiration of a recess appointee’s tenure and petitioned for review in January 2012.

Following another denial on March 15, it challenged January appointments on the ground that Senate pro forma meetings interrupted any recess. The Board denied the next motion March 27 and filed the record, giving the appellate court exclusive jurisdiction under § 160(e). An April petition joined the review and enforcement proceedings.

The majority ultimately focused on the original group and Becker’s earlier appointment rather than deciding every later membership objection. Becker had been appointed March 27, 2010, during a seventeen-day intrasession break from March 26 to April 12. Unlike the January 2012 situation, the Senate indisputably was not conducting business during that actual adjournment.

sections.title: Group composition supplies the majority’s threshold inquiry
sections.cue: Explain jurisdiction, mailing, and justiciability before the constitutional rule.
paragraphs: Judge Smith, joined by Judge Van Antwerpen, relied on New Process Steel, the Supreme Court decision requiring a delegated Board group to maintain three members. A properly constituted three-member group could act with a two-member quorum, but two members could not themselves constitute the group. The majority treated statutory composition as a jurisdictional limit on adjudicatory authority that it could raise on its own at any stage. It acknowledged that an appointment objection independently could be nonjurisdictional; its theory connected invalid appointment to the statutory three-member condition.

First seeking a nonconstitutional resolution, the court rejected the argument about Liebman’s departure. The order and docket showed August 26. Later ministerial mailing did not invalidate a completed decision, and no evidence overcame regularity or justified discovery into votes or nonexistent minutes.

An amicus argued that defining recess was a presidential political question. The majority disagreed: the Clause allocated and limited power rather than committed interpretation exclusively to one branch. Courts could examine Senate procedural records and constitutional criteria without judging partisan confirmation obstruction. Political consequences did not remove that judicial task.

sections.title: The majority acknowledges textual uncertainty but finds a structural limit
sections.cue: Distinguish the three proposed meanings of recess.
paragraphs: The court separated three possibilities: intersession breaks only, those plus sufficiently long intrasession breaks, and every period when the Senate was unavailable to do business and give advice and consent. Dictionaries, parliamentary practice, state constitutions, and early executive examples did not unequivocally select intersession breaks. Some evidence favored that reading and some governors’ conduct supported intrasession appointments. The definite article alone did not decide it.

The majority instead treated nomination and Senate consent as the ordinary method, with recess appointment auxiliary. A bare unavailability test could extend to lunch, evenings, and weekends. Pro forma meetings could also conduct business, as actual passage of legislation showed, despite an initial agreement to do none. A sufficiently-long-break rule avoided some excess but lacked a constitutional basis for selecting three or ten days. Timing in the Adjournment and Pocket Veto Clauses did not simply transfer to appointments.

Its decisive inference concerned expiration at the end of the Senate’s next session. An intersession appointment lasted through one ensuing session; an intrasession appointment could span the rest of the current one and all of the next. The majority saw that as an additional appointment route after an opportunity for the ordinary process rather than merely its auxiliary. It acknowledged that the text could accommodate the longer tenure, but found the narrower construction more natural. The Constitution did not expressly prohibit appointments using the word intrasession.

sections.title: Historical practice does not persuade the majority to broaden the exception
sections.cue: Preserve acknowledged weaknesses and the exact result.
paragraphs: Early presidential practice was largely intersession, with disputed Andrew Johnson exceptions. A 1921 Attorney General opinion supported intrasession appointments, increasingly used by later Presidents. The majority considered that comparatively recent and disputed practice insufficient to revise constitutional structure, and questioned deference to executive constitutional judgments in a powers dispute.

It preferred clear intersession boundaries to functional uncertainty or an arbitrary day count while acknowledging strategic possibilities: the Senate might manipulate timing, and Presidents might appoint during extremely brief intersession gaps. It did not claim to eliminate manipulation, only to identify allocated powers.

On May 16, 2013, the panel held Becker’s intrasession appointment invalid and vacated the original and reconsideration orders because the original group lacked three lawful members. It did not decide whether the nurses were supervisors, what vacancies that “happen” meant, or the validity of the later groups’ appointments. Reconsideration did not salvage the invalid original action.

sections.title: Greenaway favors actual availability with practical limits
sections.cue: Close with the dissent and the historical boundary of this ruling.
paragraphs: Judge Greenaway would include both intersession and intrasession recesses because the Senate could be unavailable to consent in either. The text lacked an intersession modifier, and its definite article did not create one. He regarded pocket-veto decisions as useful functional analogies, not controlling appointment law.

For him, recess power kept offices filled while senators left and prevented confirmation authority from becoming an unchecked barrier to administration. Temporary tenure, Senate control of breaks, political accountability, and need for continuing cooperation constrained abuse. Lunch, overnight, and weekend absences did not qualify under his understanding. A fixed expiration point did not require equal tenure for all appointees or only one Senate opportunity to consider them.

Longstanding intrasession practice, a 1905 Senate report, changed congressional schedules, and the Pay Act supported that reading; early nonuse did not surrender power. An intersession-only rule could permit appointments in a momentary gap while denying them in a months-long absence merely because of procedural labels. Greenaway treated pro forma periods as functionally continuous and would uphold Becker and the identified January appointees. Separately, he rejected calling group membership jurisdictional, noting that New Process Steel had not done so. He did not resolve the nurses’ status.

The later Supreme Court Noel Canning decision permitted intrasession appointments. This account preserves the Third Circuit’s earlier divided judgment and reasoning, not a claim that its categorical limitation remains governing law.

sources.pinpoint: Greenaway dissent 1–55 & nn.1–28; assigned later Noel Canning account
